title: The Seven Kings
objective: After this level you can outline Rome’s age of kings and how kingship worked there.
summary: Seven kings ruled from 753 to 509 BCE, each chosen with the Senate’s and people’s approval. Numa founded religion; Servius, the census.

cards.headline: Rome had seven kings, if you trust the legends. Not the kind you picture.
cards.body: No crown passed neatly from father to son. Most of the time, Rome had other ideas about who got the job.

cards.headline: Seven kings
cards.body: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus in 753 BCE to Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, the last three of them Etruscans. But this wasn’t a family business. Kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people. Being the old king’s son didn’t get you the job. Getting approved did.

cards.headline: Remembered for different things
cards.body: Each king came with a reputation, like a line on a résumé. Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and its calendar. Servius Tullius, the sixth, was credited with the first census, which sorted citizens by wealth. Ask a Roman who started a custom, and there was often a king ready to take the credit.

cards.fact: The Senate started as the king’s advisers.
cards.context: It began as a council of elders who advised the king. Keep an eye on it. The kings would go, but the Senate would stay, long after the last king was gone.
